I had dabbled a bit, but they were really my inspiration and gave me and I think a lot of other people the courage to actually do it. We all wanted to be like the Beatles. I wrote two songs and the record company we were with turned down one of the songs. The song they turned down was 'For Your Love', which eventually found its way to the Yardbirds."

Gouldman's manager, Harvey Lisberg, was so impressed by the song he told Gouldman they should offer it to the Beatles. "I said, 'I think they're doing alright in the songwriting department, actually", Gouldman recalled. Undeterred, Lisberg gave a demo of the song to publisher Ronnie Beck of Feldman's, who took it to the Hammersmith Odeon, where the Beatles were performing. By coincidence the Yardbirds were also performing on a Christmas show at the venue and Beck played the song to their manager, Giorgio Gomelsky, and the band.

In 1965, the Mockingbirds began a regular warm-up spot for BBC TV's Top of the Pops, transmitted from Manchester. Gouldman recalled: "There was one strange moment when the Yardbirds appeared on the show doing 'For Your Love'. Everyone clamoured around them – and there I was just part of an anonymous group. I felt strange that night, hearing them play my song."

The Yardbirds recorded "For Your Love" at the IBC Studios in London on 1 February 1965. The majority of the song was recorded with singer Keith Relf and drummer Jim McCarty backed by session musician Ron Prentice on bowed bass, Denny Piercy on bongos, and organist Brian Auger on harpsichord. Guitarists Eric Clapton and Chris Dreja only perform during the song's double-time middle break section. Bassist Paul Samwell-Smith assumed the production duties and is listed as musical director on the 45. At the conclusion of the session, Auger wondered, "Who, in their right mind, is going to buy a pop single with harpsichord on it?"

Shortly after its release by Columbia on 5 March 1965, it became a hit in the UK. When it was released a month later by Epic Records in the US, it became the group's first charting single. By then, Clapton had already left the group for various reasons, including their more commercial aspirations.

I was born severely autistic to a psychologist father in 1969. I am mostly normal now. I have lingering symptoms of head banging and hand flailing, but usually only when I become extremely agitated. I am not an expert in Autism, but here's what I can relate based on some of my Dad's writings and some of the things that he told me:

1.) Do not become frustrated with his lack of responsiveness, or his responding in an extremely agitated way. Furthermore, do not take his shutting out reality personally. (He's not aloof or ignoring you. People tend to respond with neglect or sadism.)

2.) If you institutionalize him, you can't unboil that egg.

3.) Help reconnect him with his senses. It he becomes extremely agitated, the problem isn't the stimulation, but it is his strategy of managing it by violently distracting himself. He needs to let himself experience that which he is shutting out. He needs to know that it's okay to let himself experience the stimulation in question. Basically, they are splitting themselves from sensation through withdrawal or violent distraction. You have to interrupt that strategy, and do things to reconnect them to those sensations and to integrate that into their ongoing experience.

4.) Touching them isn't bad. They may fight it, but they need the oxytocin to trust enough to not divorce their mind from their current experience. Experts say "Blah blah blah, you shouldn't touch them because they don't like to be touched." No. Some kinds of touching work better than others. If you have to fight them to give them a hug, they will realize it is safe and stop struggling eventually. Do not do this when someone who will try to "rescue" the child is present, because they will just reaffirm the child's fears. Tickling on the back and scalp are excellent. Try to build up trust before diving right into the touching, though. A head massage may be a good substitute to interrupt head banging with.

5.) Sports and coordinated physical activity are important. He's going to be bad at it, but he will benefit the most from it. Start with just playing catch. Even if it is just rolling a ball along the floor. If they are freaking out violently trying to drive sensation from their mind, take them running. It's a good outlet. They will be bad at sports, but they need it the most. The coordination of mind and body does the most to reconnect them to their senses.

6.) Activities that demand his attention to his senses and that externally engage his attention without imagination are helpful.

7.) Distracting them when they get lost in a fantasy/daydream is helpful. Teachers are going to want to hold him back for daydreaming too much. If you let them do this, the classroom will become even less interesting than the daydream.

8.) Play language games with them a lot. Make punny dad jokes and joke around with the meaning of your words a lot. Reading "The Structure of Magic" may help. Teach them to understand multiple interpretations of surface structure until they start doing it on their own.
